query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small (≈5 at.%) amount of Sn to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will induce the formation of a continuous, Sn‐rich interfacial layer during oxidation that acts as an effective diffusion barrier against oxygen, thereby reducing pest oxidation at high temperature without sacrificing the alloy’s intrinsic room‐temperature ductility and high‐temperature strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy that shows 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C but suffers from rapid oxygen uptake (poor oxidation resistance).
generation.intervention: Alloying modification via the addition of about 5 at.% Sn to the base alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at temperatures between 800 °C and 1000 °C for durations up to 200 hours; mechanical testing (tensile tests) performed at room temperature and 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent Sn‐rich interfacial layer (or Sn‐rich compounds) at the oxide scale/substrate interface.
generation.mechanism: Sn is expected to promote a selective oxidation process that forms a Sn‐rich interlayer. This layer would slow oxygen ingress by acting as a diffusion barrier and helping to stabilize the oxide scale against spallation (as observed in related Nb-silicide systems). The key is that a limited Sn addition should not disturb the beneficial phase structure that gives the base alloy its good mechanical response.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the alloy with 5 at.% Sn is predicted to show a significantly lower oxidation weight gain and more adherent, protective oxide scales during high-temperature exposure (up to 1000 °C) while retaining similar room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy that displays acceptable mechanical performance but inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.boundary: The proposed mechanism is expected to be effective primarily under oxidation conditions in air at 800–1000 °C and for exposure times up to about 200 hours; effects at much higher temperatures or in more aggressive atmospheres are not predicted.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal builds on evidence from studies in Nb-silicide based alloys where 5 at.% Sn addition suppressed pest oxidation (see PMC6981790::web::002::1_introduction and PMC8715753::web::054::4_3_2_oxidation), while recognizing that Sn’s influence on the complex phase equilibria of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is not yet established. There is uncertainty regarding whether the beneficial Sn-induced scale stabilization observed in those systems will translate to this particular alloy without degrading its mechanical properties, as some studies (e.g., PMC6981790::web::066::6_concluding_remarks) noted possible high-temperature spallation issues.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of the baseline equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another set modified with ≈5 at.% Sn (adjusting the overall composition accordingly). Expose both sets to isothermal oxidation tests in air at 800 °C and 1000 °C for intervals ranging from 5 h to 200 h. In parallel, perform room-temperature tensile ductility tests and high-temperature strength measurements (at 1000 °C) for both compositions.
measurements: Weight gain per unit surface area during oxidation
Characterization of the scale and substrate interface via SEM/TEM to identify formation and continuity of any Sn-rich interfacial layer
Room-temperature tensile ductility (percentage elongation, fracture characteristics)
Yield strength and stress–strain behavior at 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-modified alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain and improvement in oxide scale adhesion (for instance, if comparable or worse pest oxidation is observed) or if the room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength degrades notably relative to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. This research was motivated by the need to understand how Sn improves the oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys. We discussed the selection of the Sn concentration in Nb-silicide based alloys of the Nb-Ti-Si-Al-Cr-Sn system and presented the results of a systematic study of three alloys of nominal compositions, namely Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Cr-5Sn (ZX4), Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Sn (ZX6), and Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Cr-5Sn (ZX8). There was macrosegregation in all three alloys that was most severe in ZX8. The Nbss was not stable in ZX6, the Nb3Sn was stable in all three alloys and the Nbss and the C14-NbCr2 Laves phase were stable in ZX4 and ZX8. In all three alloys, the primary βNb5Si3 transformed completely to αNb5Si3 after heat treatment. The 5 at.% Sn addition suppressed pest oxidation at 800 °C, but not the spallation of scales at 1200 °C. At 800 and 1200 °C, a Sn-rich area developed below the scale in the substrate/scale interface where Nb3Sn, Nb5Sn2Si and NbSn2 compounds were formed. The latter two compounds were most noticeable at 1200 °C. The Sn-rich area was thicker at 1200 °C and was contaminated by oxygen at both temperatures.
